sourceLine: Reuters, Mar 2021 · AlixPartners, Sep 2021 · Overall shortage impact, not fire-only loss
notes: In March 2021, fire hit Renesas, a firm supplying about thirty percent of automotive microcontrollers. That concentration exposed how one upstream facility could affect many manufacturers. Separately, AlixPartners estimated the entire 2021 chip shortage cost automakers two hundred and ten billion dollars and seven point seven million vehicles. We are not attributing that whole loss to one fire. The lesson is that a small-looking upstream dependency can become a system-wide production problem.

sourceLine: McKinsey [report details VERIFY] · McKinsey 2022 · McKinsey Supply Chain Risk Survey 2024
notes: The iceberg is the problem. About two-thirds of disruptions originate at tier two or deeper, according to McKinsey. Only about ten percent of firms see their tier-three suppliers, and the average response to a new disruption is about two weeks. These measures come from different published observations, not one experiment. ShockTwin asks a practical question: can a buyer identify a consequential hidden dependency and act while inventory still gives them time?

support: Mapping upstream dependencies can turn a hidden concentration into a decision.
imagePrompt: Cinematic painterly matte painting, hand-painted animation and classical landscape influences, slightly surreal yet coherent, 16:9 landscape, at least 1920x1080. notes: There is a useful counterexample. After 2011, Toyota mapped about fifteen hundred critical parts. During the chip crisis it kept US production near ninety percent, while GM cut about two hundred and seventy-eight thousand units. The cited reporting does not prove that mapping alone caused that difference. It shows why upstream knowledge deserves attention. Our aim is to make mapping actionable through a connected warning, rehearsal and response workflow.

sourceLine: Illustrative local simulation · Assumptions and real app result in screenshot
notes: Now we rehearse the cyclone. This is the real simulator, using illustrative inputs: eighteen hundred resin units and demand of one hundred units per day. Under the default full-loss shock, baseline stock reaches zero on day eighteen. Switch on replacement flow after day three, and the curve holds at fifteen hundred units because replacement covers daily demand. That avoids a line stop through this displayed horizon. It is conditional on timing, volume and availability, not a promise of endless continuity. We can change severity, duration and switch timing to see where the plan fails.
